Assume full AC. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be compact smooth embedded spanning surfaces for the same nonempty link $L$, with supplied radial collars in disjoint smooth normal tubes of $L$. Orient each component of $L$ arbitrarily, orient the tube boundary tori by their outward normal toward the link exterior, and orient the two surface boundary curves compatibly with $L$. Let $\alpha$ be a smooth proper transverse common arc in the exterior, transverse to its boundary, with transverse boundary-curve crossings at its distinct endpoints. Extend it radially to an isolated smooth embedded arc $A$ ending on $L$. Suppose its two ordered endpoint intersection signs agree, so their sum is $2$ or $-2$.

For every open neighborhood $U$ of $A$ there are a smooth closed ball $B\subset U$ with $A\subset\operatorname{int}B$ and a continuous surjection $q:S^3\to S^3$, fixed off $\operatorname{int}B$, such that its only non-singleton fiber is $A$, $q(B)=B$, and
$$(B,q((F_0\cup F_1)\cap B))\cong(B^3,B^3\cap\{z=0\}).$$
Thus this actual local surface image is a properly embedded locally flat disk, including at the collapsed point. The surfaces may be disconnected or nonorientable. No definiteness or primeness assumption is needed for this local assertion.

Take four rectangles $P_j=[0,1]_t\times[0,1]_r$, $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. Identify their edges $r=0$ pointwise in the $t$ coordinate to a common arc $A$. At each end $t=e$, $e\in\{0,1\}$, also identify the radial edges pointwise in $r$ by a matching $\mu_e$, where each $\mu_e$ is one of $M=(01)(23)$ and $N=(03)(12)$. Let $K$ be this finite quotient complex, and let $C$ be the image of the four outer edges $r=1$.

If the two end matchings differ, then $K/A$ is a closed topological disk whose boundary is exactly the image of $C$, and the collapsed arc is an interior point of that disk. If the two end matchings agree, then $K/A$ is two closed disks joined at their interior centers, so it is not a topological two-manifold at the collapsed point. Explicitly, $K/A$ is the cone on the graph $C$; the latter is one four-edge circle for distinct matchings and two disjoint two-edge circles for equal matchings.

Consequently, if a finite Hausdorff two-dimensional cell complex is already a topological two-manifold away from finitely many disjoint arc subcomplexes, with neighborhoods modeled by the interiors $r<1$ of these four-page models with distinct end matchings, collapsing those arcs gives a topological two-manifold. No boundary is created at a collapsed point. Collapsing any finite disjoint arc subcomplexes preserves the Euler characteristic, whether or not the local end matchings differ. These are intrinsic topological conclusions; an ambient embedding or local flatness needs separate data.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $N$ be a compact codimension-zero $C^2$ subsurface of a Hausdorff second-countable boundaryless $C^2$ surface $S$, with $C^2$ boundary. Let $G\subset\operatorname{Int}N$ be a finite embedded graph: its vertices are distinct points, each edge is a regular $C^2$ embedded arc up to its endpoints, and different edge interiors are disjoint and avoid the vertices. Closed regular edges may first be subdivided by inserting finitely many vertices. Then $N$ has a finite triangular cellulation containing $G\cup\partial N$ in its one-skeleton. Each closed triangle is an embedded topological disk, the prescribed graph and original boundary retain their regular $C^2$ arcs, and the cell maps induce a homeomorphism from a finite abstract simplicial complex onto $N$ after finite subdivision. Interior edges have two incident triangles and boundary edges one; vertex links are circles or intervals, respectively.

A cell map is required to be a homeomorphism; the statement does not assert a differentiable straightening of an arbitrary prescribed graph at its vertices. This permits tangencies between prescribed edge germs. The empty $N$ or empty $G$ is allowed.
For a finite CW complex, $\chi(X)=\sum_n(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}H_n(X;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every nonempty compact
connected boundaryless topological $2$-manifold is homeomorphic to exactly one
of the following types: the sphere $S^2$, a connected sum of $g\geq1$ tori,
or a connected sum of $k\geq1$ real projective planes. The connected sums here
are the explicit polygonal models with their chosen disk removals and boundary
gluings ([[def-connected-sum-of-compact-surfaces]]). The integer is unique
within its type. Equivalently, two such surfaces are homeomorphic if and only
if they have the same integral orientability and Euler characteristic.

The canonical one-face words are respectively the sphere digon $aa^{-1}$
(whose *reduced notation* is empty), the $g$-fold commutator word
$\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1} b_i^{-1}$, and the $k$-fold square word
$\prod_{j=1}^k c_jc_j$. The empty notation is not an empty polygonal schema.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] in pairwise disjoint balls $B_j$ inside the prescribed neighborhoods. Compose the finitely many resulting maps. They preserve their respective balls and are the identity outside them, so their supports do not interfere. The composite $q$ is onto, and its nonsingleton fibers are precisely the $A_j$; it induces a homeomorphism from the ambient quotient onto $S^3$, since the quotient is compact and the target Hausdorff. At each collapsed point the entire local image of $F_0\cup F_1$ is the disk in [F1]. Away from the arcs, a point of just one surface has its ordinary smooth disk chart. At a point of $L$ away from arc endpoints, the radial collars give two distinct rays in each normal disk. They are distinct because equality would give a common radial segment not contained in the listed arcs. Locally along a short interval of $L$, choose continuous angular lifts of those two rays. The increasing piecewise-linear angular map sending them to angles zero and $\pi$, linear on each of the two intervening angular intervals, gives a homeomorphism of the normal disk, continuous along the interval and at its center. Thus their two half-sheets form a locally flat disk. These charts cover the image, which is consequently a compact locally flat embedded closed topological surface $S$.

Produce compatible finite cells before computing Euler characteristic. Double each $F_i$ along its boundary using its smooth collar. On the boundaryless double the graph $G=L\cup\bigcup_j A_j$ is a finite embedded regular graph: put vertices at every arc endpoint and at least one on every remaining link circle. The arcs meet the boundary transversely in the original surface boundary charts, and the graph is contained in the interior of the double. Apply [F3] with the whole double as its compact subsurface. Since $L$ lies in the resulting one-skeleton, the triangles on either side of $L$ restrict to a finite cellulation of the original $F_i$, relative to $G$. Refine the two finite subdivisions of each common graph edge to their union, extending a boundary-edge subdivision across each incident triangle by a finite fan. Both cellulations then restrict to the same cells on the actual graph. Glue them using their actual pointwise identification on $G$. The resulting finite disk attachments give a finite CW structure on $K=F_0\cup F_1$: the quotient of the disjoint compact surfaces by these identifications is homeomorphic to their Hausdorff embedded union. No claim of smooth or affine gluing at a vertex is needed.

For each connected component of either $F_i$, its triangulation has a boundary edge. In a cellular integral two-cycle, the coefficient of the incident triangle must vanish, because that boundary edge has only one incident triangle. Across an interior edge the two incident coefficients differ only by an orientation sign, so vanishing propagates across it. The dual adjacency graph of the triangles is connected: paths between triangle interiors in the connected surface can be perturbed in finitely many local disk or half-disk charts to avoid the finite vertices and to cross edges finitely many times. Hence all coefficients vanish. There are no cells above dimension two, so $H_2(F_i;\mathbb Z)=0$, and all higher homology vanishes as well. Its zeroth homology has rank $p$. Formula [F4] gives $\chi(F_i)=p-b_i$, with no orientability assumption.

Let $k$ be the number of connected components of $K$. It is finite because $K$ is a union of finitely many connected surface components. Every such component contains a component of each $F_i$: any component of either $F_i$ has a boundary circle in the common $L$, and that circle belongs also to a component of the other surface. Thus $k\le p$. Collapsing an arc does not join distinct components, since that arc lies wholly in one component; the images of the finitely many disjoint compact components remain disjoint compact sets. Consequently $S$ also has exactly $k$ components.

The graph $G$ is obtained from the disjoint link circles, whose Euler characteristic is zero, by attaching the $n$ arc edges at existing vertices, allowing further subdivisions without changing the count. Thus $\chi(G)=-n$. The compatible cell structures in step 1.2 count cells of $G$ twice in $F_0$ and $F_1$ and once in their union. Therefore $\chi(K)=\chi(F_0)+\chi(F_1)-\chi(G)=2p-b_0-b_1+n=2p$. Each $A_j$ is an arc subcomplex, and the compact surface image $S$ is exactly their quotient in $K$. By [F2] it has a finite CW structure with $\chi(S)=\chi(K)=2p$.

Each component $S_a$ is a connected compact boundaryless topological surface by step 1.1. Its type in [F5] has Euler characteristic at most two, with equality only for the sphere. Explicitly the sphere digon has two vertices, one paired edge and one face, giving two; the genus-$g$ one-face polygon has one vertex and $2g$ edges, giving $2-2g$; the $k'$-crosscap polygon has one vertex and $k'$ edges, giving $2-k'$. These finite polygonal counts agree with the finite cell count of $S_a$ by [F4]. Combining the component inequalities and step 3.1 gives $2p=\sum_a\chi(S_a)\le2k\le2p$. Equality forces $k=p$ and $\chi(S_a)=2$ for every $a$. Thus all $S_a$ are spheres. Since each component already contains at least one component of each $F_i$ and there are exactly $p$ available on each side, it contains exactly one of each. All local-flatness and support assertions were proved in step 1.1; for $n=0$ the same proof uses the identity map and an empty collapse list.

boundaries.reason: The common boundary link is explicitly nonempty and every surface component has boundary.

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1 treats n=0 with the identity map; the Euler count still forces p spheres.
Step 4.1 includes p=1; no argument requires multiple components or arcs.
Step 2.1 proves H2 vanishing without orientability or a nondegenerate pairing assumption; no normal form is inverted.
Step 1.1 uses actual standard ball-disk charts at all arc endpoints and radial collar charts elsewhere on the common boundary.
The Statement assumes full AC; only the locally flat collapse, finite cellulation and surface classification suppliers carry choice uses.

boundaries.reason: The result is an implication, with no equivalence asserted.

axioms.use: Full AC is inherited from the actual locally flat arc-collapse and compact surface classification suppliers. The cell counts, component inequalities and finite composition introduce no additional choice.

risk_review.notes: Global finite-cell glue and Euler calculation supplied explicitly; no smoothness of quotient spheres, nonsplit reduction, alternating diagram reconstruction or full flyping conclusion inferred.

lem-finite-standard-arc-collapse-of-bala.proof_status_evidence: Six actual local proof rows and explicit scoped final checks; mathematical acceptance and canonical readiness remain root-owned.
